body_markdown:
In the realm of prewar American cars, all manner of Ford Model Ts and As are near and dear to many enthusiasts, and for good reason. But here we’re toasting something[out of the ordinary](https://www.hagerty.com/media/car-profiles/decades-later-a-wayward-32-plymouth-finds-its-way-home/) —a car that began life as a 1934 Plymouth coupe. From its distinctive hood ornament to its vintage Michigan license plate, the rat rod Eric Souva built at home shouts *extra* ordinary.


*Welcome to **Homegrown** —a series about homebuilt cars and the ingenuity of their visionary creators. Know a car and builder that might fit the bill? Send us an email at[tips@hagerty.com](https://www.hagerty.com/mailto:tips@hagerty.com) with the subject line HOMEGROWN.[Read about more Homegrown creations here](https://www.hagerty.com/media/tags/homegrown/) . —Ed.*


Souva, 50, explains his life and times: “I grew up on a Michigan farm. After high school, I worked at a large automotive manufacturing plant, until it closed in 2007. My wife Kim and I raised three sons on our 11-acre farm near Carlton, Michigan, where we reside with nine chickens, three horses, and the occasional coyote.


Don Sherman


“In 2021, I founded K and E Kustoms to do body and paint work in my 32×40-foot pole barn. The last five years I’ve focused on repairing ATVs and motorcycles. Of course, there’s always time for personal jobs such as my custom ’67 Chevy pickup and the 1925 Ford Speedster hot rod I built in 2013.


“Four years ago, I spotted this ’34 Plymouth at a car meet in Bowling Green, Ohio. A title and the frame were included but many parts were missing—the entire driveline and suspension; fenders; the floor and rocker panels; and the roof’s filler panel. It was marketed as a jalopy for drag racing. I paid $2500 and hauled my find home with no specific plan in mind.


“A year later, my wife insisted I get busy building *something* within a $10,000 budget.


“I MIG-welded a new frame, providing a 128-inch wheelbase, from 2×4-inch steel tubing. A 4×8-foot steel sheet was cut and shaped to replace the missing panels behind the cabin. I fabricated new rocker panels from the curved steel runs used to support garage doors. To highlight my rat rod’s rough and tumble spirit, I left a few original leaded body spots unpainted. Strips of factory wood framing inside the roof pillars are also visible. While the ’34 grille shell is in decent shape, I had to shorten it 10 inches for this application.


Don Sherman


“An exotic front suspension consisting of longitudinal arms pivoted by Airmax air-bag inflators provides the motion to drop my frame to the ground for static display. I bought that, along with a two-link air-bag rear suspension, from Village Customs of Raleigh, North Carolina. My front beam axle came from a ’59 Chevy pickup, while the rear end is a ’96 Chevy pickup axle with a 3.55:1 differential ratio. My steering gear is from a Chevy Corvair.


“I bought Boyd Coddington steel wheels from the Jeg’s catalog. My General G-Max radials are 235/55-17s in front and the rears are 265/50-20s.


Don Sherman


“I found my 383-cubic-inch, 345-horsepower[Mopar V-8](https://www.hagerty.com/media/maintenance-and-tech/powerful-statement-crate-engines-could-solve-your-problem/) in Sandusky, Ohio. It drives a three-speed 727 automatic transmission and is cooled by a custom aluminum radiator intended for a Ford Falcon. My nephew, one of the best welders in the country, fabricated the straight-through exhaust headers.


“My cockpit is fitted with half a dozen Dolphin instruments. The 140-mph speedometer works off GPS so no drive cable is needed. Brake and throttle pedals came from Wilwood. A pair of AFCO master cylinders operate my vented disc brakes.


“I found bomber bucket seats on display at a Michigan auto show. They’re both attractive and reasonably comfortable; given their $1400 cost, they should be! My homemade cushions are upholstered with marine-grade vinyl to help them resist rain damage. Ample ventilation is provided by the original Plymouth windshield, which hinges open along its top surface.


“I bought my floor and sidewall trim materials at Lowe’s. Bottom panels are SnapLock topped by plywood and then vinyl planking. A 14-gallon fuel cell is mounted under the rear compartment’s floor.


Don Sherman


“There are a couple of finishing touches worth mentioning: The original hood ornament depicting a Mayflower sailing ship cost $414 on eBay! My 1934 Michigan license plate, also obtained via eBay, is still legitimate for road use. The deck lid’s lift handle is a connecting rod from a Polaris Ranger RZR ATV.”


Asked to estimate the total time and cost invested in his Plymouth, Souva reveals: “Having spent $13,000 or so on parts, I did exceed my wife’s budget, but she is satisfied with the results. Of course, that figure doesn’t include hundreds of hours of my labor. Start to finish, this project lasted two and a half years. Thus far, my wife and I have driven it 1600 miles to car gatherings.”


When I asked Souva for a test drive in his pride and joy, he didn’t flinch at the request. The first challenge was getting in, because the driver’s outside door handle doesn’t work and an interior bungee cord keeps the door latched. Before I cranked the engine, Souva warned me about lots of lash in the steering, which he has been unable to remove. Then I had to swing the windshield shut because, when open, its bottom edge blocked my view of the road ahead.


Don Sherman


Unmuffled horses are anxious to trot the instant the ignition key is twisted. An intoxicating rumble arrives when the throttle is lifted a touch. The effort required to manipulate the steering is high by today’s standards, proving that this ’34 is no sports car. We move slowly out of the driveway and onto local pavement with no traffic.


When I nail the throttle, Souva maintains his composure as we rocket smartly through the gears. Turning the wood-rimmed wheel, the considerable center lash poses no serious issue. Staying in one lane is largely a matter of letting the car guide itself.


Don Sherman


We encounter no serious bumps, so the nicely damped air springs provide a placid ride. Pedal tromped to the wood, we top out at around 75 mph, the maximum speed Souva experiences traveling to car shows via freeway. While higher velocities are well within reach, wearing out my welcome is one mistake I carefully avoid.


The brakes repeatedly slow us without trauma. Turning back toward home, the heavy steering effort is again noticeable, reminding me of the strides achieved by modern cars.


It’s perfectly clear why Souva’s car often wins a trophy at rat rod gatherings: It is great looking, solidly constructed, and a nice break from commonplace Ford Model Ts and As.
